orders.description: Plaintiffs’ appeal from the June 13, 2017 summary-judgment dismissal.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: The injured plaintiff allegedly caught her right foot under a tire/wheel stop and tripped in the parking lot of a Dunkin’ Donuts restaurant in Oyster Bay. Defendants allegedly owned, operated and/or maintained the restaurant; the precise allocation among defendants is not stated.

legal_issues.finding: Defendants argued noncreation; the specified appellate ground is deficient constructive-notice proof, without a separate creation determination.
Defendants argued lack of actual notice; the opinion does not separately resolve actual notice.

Defendants failed to establish lack of constructive notice because they supplied no evidence of when the specific wheel stop was last inspected before the accident. The court did not conclusively find notice.

evidence_discussed.description: Evidence of the last pre-accident inspection of this wheel stop was missing. The opinion does not identify a particular testimony or records format.

quality.notes: The identified restaurant parking lot and alleged ownership/operation/maintenance support private control while preserving the allegation and role alternatives. owner/other describe alleged owner/operator/maintainer roles collectively, not proof that each defendant held every role. Injured role and accident date are unstated. Neither a specific wheel-stop defect nor its dimensions are supplied. No open-and-obvious, trivial-defect or actual-notice finding is inferred. Missing inspection timing does not identify missing inspection records specifically.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is reversed, on the law, with costs, and the defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint is denied.

Marie Troina (hereinafter the injured plaintiff) alleges that she tripped and fell when she caught her right foot under a tire/wheel stop in the parking lot of a Dunkin' Donuts restaurant in Oyster Bay. At the time, the restaurant allegedly was owned, operated, and/or maintained by the defendants Canyon Donuts Jericho Turnpike, Inc., Ronald Portnoy, and Ernest Rauch (hereinafter collectively the defendants).

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, etc., the plaintiffs appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Queens County (Janice A. Taylor, J.), dated June 13, 2017. The order granted the defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

After joinder of issue, the defendants moved for summary judgment dismissing the complaint on the ground, inter alia, that they did not create or have actual or constructive notice of the allegedly dangerous condition.

The defendants failed to establish, prima facie, that they lacked constructive notice of the allegedly dangerous condition. They failed to submit evidence as to when, prior to the accident, the tire/wheel stop at issue was last inspected

Since the defendants failed to demonstrate their prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law, the Supreme Court should have denied their motion, without regard to the sufficiency of the opposition papers

orders.description: Defendant’s appeal from the May 8, 2019 denial of summary judgment.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied defendant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly fell in the lobby of defendant’s building in Queens on April 7, 2016. She surmised that she tripped on a defective runner mat but testified she saw no defect before or after falling, although she traversed the lobby practically every work day.

legal_issues.finding: Plaintiff’s deposition established inability to identify the cause without speculation; the unobserved alleged runner-mat defect was insufficient and opposition raised no triable issue.

evidence_discussed.description: Defendant submitted plaintiff’s deposition; she did not see the alleged mat defect before or after the fall.

quality.notes: Defendant’s building does not expressly establish private ownership/control or building subtype; the LLC name and work-day traversal do not cure that uncertainty. The trip mechanism is expressly alleged in P003 even though its cause is speculative; unsuccessful causation proof alone does not defeat scope. other hazard denotes the alleged defective mat, whose specific defect is not described or established. Work-day traversal does not establish an employee role. Generic creation/notice standards in P002 are not separate case-specific determinations. Reversal granting defense dismissal is clear; property review alone keeps the binary label null.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is reversed, on the law, with costs, and the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint is granted.
On April 7, 2016, the plaintiff allegedly fell inside the lobby of the defendant's building in Queens.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the defendant appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Queens County (Leslie J. Purificacion, J.), entered May 8, 2019. The order denied the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

Here, the defendant established its prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law through, inter alia, the deposition testimony of the plaintiff, which demonstrated that she could not identify the cause of her fall without resorting to speculation

The plaintiff surmised that she tripped and fell on a defective part of a runner mat that was located in the lobby of the defendant's building. However, the plaintiff, who traversed this lobby practically every work day, testified that she did not see the alleged defect either before or after she fell.
In opposition to the defendant's prima facie showing, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact.
Accordingly, the Supreme Court should have granted the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint

orders.description: Defendant’s limited appeal from the November 3, 2010 pre-answer dismissal ruling.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied the appealed portions of defendant’s CPLR 3211(a)(1) and (7) motion to dismiss the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiffs alleged in a wrongful-death action that decedent slipped and fell while working at premises owned by nonparty 21 Club, Inc. That company was owned by 21 Club Properties, Inc., which was in turn owned by defendant; the hazard, exact accident location and decedent’s employment arrangement are not stated.

legal_issues.finding: The remaining evidence did not irrefutably negate defendant’s ownership/control of the premises, the basis of the pleaded liability. Corporate control and premises control were distinguished; ownership/control by defendant was not finally found.
Affidavit and deposition testimony did not qualify as documentary evidence under CPLR 3211(a)(1); the factual alter-ego question could not be resolved on this pre-answer motion.

The Workers’ Compensation Law exclusivity argument was rejected: liability was premised on premises ownership/control rather than control of 21 Club, and the asserted alter-ego relationship also presented an unresolved factual issue.

evidence_discussed.description: Defendant offered an affidavit and deposition testimony, rejected as documentary evidence for CPLR 3211(a)(1). Authors/deponent are unspecified. The other evidence was insufficient to conclusively negate ownership/control; its format is not identified.

quality.notes: Explicit ownership of the accident premises by nonparty 21 Club supports private premises; defendant’s own ownership/control remains disputed. This is a substantive dismissal appeal on premises responsibility and a compensation-exclusivity defense, with ancillary evidentiary rules, not a procedural-only or third-party-only dispute. The limited appeal is wholly affirmed. Working is explicit, but the precise employee/contractor status and employer are not established; injured_role=other preserves that distinction. defendant_roles=other records the expressly identified corporate grandparent, not proven ownership of the premises. Neither restaurant use nor a hazard is inferred from corporate names. Workers’ Compensation Law is recorded under other, not labor_law. OCR in the quoted defense standard is preserved.

evidence.quote: Order, Supreme Court, Bronx County (Norma Ruiz, J.), entered November 3, 2010, which, insofar as appealed from as limited by the briefs, denied defendant’s pre-answer motion to dismiss the complaint pursuant to CPLR 3211 (a) (1) and (7), unanimously affirmed, without costs.

In this wrongful death action, plaintiffs allege that decedent slipped and fell while working in premises owned by nonparty 21 Club, Inc,, which is wholly-owned by nonparty 21 Club Properties, Inc., which, in turn, is wholly-owned by defendant.
Neither the affidavit nor the deposition testimony defendant offered constitutes the type of documentary evidence that may be considered on a motion pursuant to CPLR 3211 (a) (1)

The remainder of the evidence does not “conclusively establish! ] a defense to the asserted claims as a matter of law” because it does not irrefutably establish that defendant neither owned nor controlled the premises

We reject defendant’s argument that, even if it controlled 21 Club, Inc. and thus can be considered its alter ego, this action would still be barred by the exclusivity provisions of the Workers’ Compensation Law. Defendant’s liability is premised upon its ownership and/or control of the premises, not its ownership and/or control of 21 Club, Inc. Accordingly, whether or not defendant is the alter ego of 21 Club, Inc. is irrelevant.
Further, defendant’s argument relies upon a factual issue, whether it controlled 21 Club, Inc. and thus constituted its alter ego, which cannot be determined on this pre-answer motion to dismiss.

orders.description: Plaintiff’s appeal from the May 15, 2012 order resolving motion and cross-motion.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted defendant’s summary-judgment dismissal and denied plaintiff’s cross-motion for summary judgment on liability.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped on the back steps of defendant’s residence. She testified that she felt a hard cone or ball underfoot, then saw a crushed golf-ball-sized seed ball and other seed balls and leaves on the steps and landing, apparently from a neighbor’s tree.

legal_issues.finding: Defendant established that the seed-ball/leaf condition was readily observable and not inherently dangerous; plaintiff raised no triable issue. Both elements support dismissal.

evidence_discussed.description: Plaintiff described what she felt before the fall and the seed balls/leaves observed afterward.

quality.notes: Defendant’s residence and its back steps support private residential control without establishing legal title or tenancy; defendant_roles stays unclear. Plaintiff’s visitor/guest status is unstated. The single appealed order resolves two motions, so multiple_orders=false. The apparent tree source is not made certain, and the golf-ball-sized seed ball is not a separate trivial-defect holding. No creation, notice or expert analysis is inferred.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.
The plaintiff allegedly was injured when she slipped and fell on the back steps of the defendant’s residence.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Richmond County (Maltese, J.), dated May 15, 2012, which granted the defendant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint and denied her cross motion for summary judgment on the issue of liability.

The plaintiff testified that, prior to her fall, she felt a “hard cone” or “ball” underneath her foot. After her fall, she observed a crushed seed ball, about the size of a golf ball, on the step. Two or three other seed balls and some leaves were scattered about the steps and landing. The seed balls and leaves apparently had fallen from a nearby tree belonging to the defendant’s neighbor.

The defendant made a prima facie showing that the complained-of condition was both open and obvious, i.e., readily observable by those employing the reasonable use of their senses, and not inherently dangerous
In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact.

Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly granted the defendant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint and denied the plaintiffs cross motion for summary judgment on the issue of liability.

orders.description: Defendants’ appeal from the September 4, 2013 denial of dismissal.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the amended complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly tripped over boxes left in the meat aisle of defendants’ supermarket and alleged that defendants negligently left them there.

legal_issues.finding: The court applied the rule that no duty to protect or warn attaches to an open and obvious condition that is not inherently dangerous.
Plaintiff alleged defendants negligently left the boxes; the court resolved dismissal on obviousness and lack of inherent danger without separately determining placement.
Defendants established that the boxes were readily observable and not inherently dangerous; plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue.

quality.notes: The supermarket’s actual meat aisle supports private retail control without establishing ownership or lease status. Injured customer status is not inferred solely from the setting. The court identifies no evidence formats, box dimensions, inspection times or accident date. Obviousness and lack of inherent danger are both stated, not inferred from citations. Alleged placement by defendants remains an allegation rather than a separate creation finding.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is reversed, on the law, with costs, and the defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the amended complaint is granted.
The plaintiff allegedly was injured when she tripped and fell over boxes left in the meat aisle of the defendants' supermarket.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the defendants appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Queens County (Lebowitz, J.), entered September 4, 2013, which denied their motion for summary judgment dismissing the amended complaint.
She commenced this action to recover damages for personal injuries against the defendants alleging, inter alia, that they negligently left the boxes in the supermarket aisle.
However, there is no duty to protect or warn against an open and obvious condition which, as a matter of law, is not inherently dangerous

Here, the defendants established their prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law by demonstrating that the subject boxes in the supermarket aisle were open and obvious (i.e., readily observable by the reasonable use of one's senses), and not inherently dangerous
In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact.
Accordingly, the Supreme Court should have granted the defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the amended complaint.
